problems.title: Coordinate pooling does not give coordinatewise or joint coverage
problems.source_location: Current paper, Remark 1 and Eqs. (9)–(11), pp. 5–6; vector coverage Eq. (13), p. 8; segmentation description, p. 9.
claim: Pooled coordinate calibration inherits coordinatewise and whole-vector coverage.
analysis: Take \(n=99\), \(d=11\), \(\alpha=0.1\), and deterministic IID vectors \(Y=(0,\ldots,0,1)\). Let \(h(X)=0\) and \(g(v)=v\), so predictions are zero but all Jacobian row norms are one. Pooling the coordinate scores gives \(990\) zeros and \(99\) ones. Even the finite-rank index \(\lceil1090\cdot0.9\rceil=981\) selects zero. Thus the last coordinate and the whole-vector event have coverage zero, while coordinate-average coverage is \(10/11>90\%\).
result: Exchangeability across sample vectors does not imply exchangeability of their coordinates. The example refutes fixed-coordinate and simultaneous-vector guarantees, but preserves the weaker average-coordinate interpretation and the scalar rank proof.
assumptions: Only the author-released source version and stated claim are assessed.
repair: Calibrate each preselected coordinate from its \(n\) sample scores, or calibrate a per-vector maximum score for simultaneous coverage. Specify which event is intended.
problems.impact_rationale: A legal exchangeable vector distribution has zero coverage for the claimed fixed-coordinate and whole-vector events. The central multidimensional coverage extension fails.
problems.existing_correction_status: Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Shortest-layer selection breaks the fixed-score guarantee
problems.source_location: Current paper, Table 2 caption, p. 7, and evaluation rule, p. 8; author FastFeatureCP/main.py, lines 99–111 and result selection.
claim: The shortest empirically selected layer retains the fixed-score conformal guarantee.
analysis: Use one calibration sample and target coverage \(1/2\). Let \(X\in\{A,B\}\) be equiprobable, \(Y\sim U(0,1)\), and \(f=0\). Two fixed-layer scales are \((1,100)\) and \((100,1)\) on \((A,B)\). Each fixed layer has exact marginal coverage \(1/2\). Selecting the shorter interval gives coverage \(\frac12\cdot\frac12+\frac12\cdot\frac1{200}=0.2525\).

These scales can arise in one network: take \(T(x,z)=(x,a(x)z)\), \(g(x,u)=b(x)u\), with \(z=0\), \(a(A)=0.01,a(B)=100,b(A)=100,b(B)=1\). The relevant gradient norms are \(ab\) and \(b\), exactly the two scales. Conditional on the calibration group, the same layer is no wider at every test point, so choosing by any nonempty finite test set's mean length has the same failure.
result: This refutes unconditional inheritance of the fixed-layer rank guarantee. The \(25.25\%\) value is for this explicit one-calibration-sample construction, not a reproduction of the paper's datasets or nominal \(90\%\) experiment.
assumptions: Only the author-released source version and stated claim are assessed.
repair: Select the layer using data independent of final calibration/test data, freeze it, then calibrate anew; conditional exchangeability restores the fixed-score rank argument.
problems.impact_rationale: An explicit same-network example violates the claimed inheritance of fixed-layer coverage after shortest-layer selection. This affects the central validity argument, with a clearly stated scope.
problems.existing_correction_status: Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: RAPS pseudocode reverses quantile order
problems.source_location: Current paper, Algorithm 5, steps 3–4, p. 22; author FastFeatureRAPS/conformal.py, line 225 uses the upper quantile instead.
claim: The RAPS order-statistic direction gives the upper conformal threshold.
analysis: Algorithm 5 requests the \(k=\lceil(1-\alpha)(n+1)\rceil\)-th largest score. At \(n=99,\alpha=0.1\), this is the tenth smallest, instead of the ninetieth smallest. Take \(K=100\), \(h(X)=0\), \(g(v)=\operatorname{softmax}(cv)\), with \(c=K/\sqrt{K-1}\). Every class probability is \(1/K\), and each Jacobian row has norm \(1/\sqrt K=0.1\), so the example does not rely on a zero gradient. Set \(\delta=0\) and \(k_{\mathrm{reg}}=100\), making the nonnegative rank penalty inactive. Break prediction ties by one fixed class order. A random permutation of one sample per class gives an exchangeable sequence. Enumerating its possible held-out test classes while retaining the algorithm’s extra-one set-size rule gives coverage \(11/100\) for the printed reverse order and \(91/100\) for ascending order. The current source uses an upper np.quantile and does not implement the printed reversal; \(11\%\) is not attributed to the published experiment.
result: The printed direction defeats the intended coverage guarantee. The author code uses an upper-tail quantile rather than this reversed order, so \(11\%\) is not assigned to the published classification tables.
assumptions: Only the author-released source version and stated claim are assessed.
repair: Use the required ascending upper order statistic and specify its finite-sample, tie and prediction-set inversion rules together.
problems.impact_rationale: The printed rank direction can reduce nominal coverage from ninety percent to eleven percent in a valid exchangeable classification construction. This substantial algorithmic derivation error meets Major even though the release code differs.
problems.existing_correction_status: Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The diagnostic omits a scale-dependent regularity constant
claim: The empirical score-concentration diagnostic verifies the regularity condition independent of units.
analysis: Use the reparameterization \(h_c=ch\), \(g_c(v)=g(v/c)\), with \(c>0\). Predictions remain unchanged; a gradient scale \(s\) becomes \(s/c\), scores \(R\) and their quantile \(q\) become \(cR\) and \(cq\), and the interval radius remains \(sq\). Absolute score concentration nevertheless changes with \(c\). The current Appendix B.2 explicitly ignores the Hölder/Lipschitz factor while comparing concentration, so that comparison alone cannot verify the complete dimensional inequality in Theorem A.1. This limits the assumption diagnostic, not the conformal interval’s invariance.
